asDecan.p: Each sign is cut into three ten-degree slices, called decans, with a planet and a small card each. Your Sun sits between 20 and 29 degrees of Aquarius, the last slice, and in the old Chaldean order that one goes to the Moon. The Moon has no special standing in Aquarius. It's a guest, neither helped nor held back, so it takes on the tone of the house's owner, Saturn in the old scheme and Uranus in the modern one. To be honest that's an odd arrangement, the planet of feelings and home lodging in a sign that likes air between people. The first slice is the Five of Swords, Venus, and the middle is the Six, Mercury's. Yours comes last and it's the most private of the three. Look at the man in the picture, tiptoeing off with an armful of swords and glancing back. The Star is your Sun card, and this is the finer grain inside it, close enough to Pisces that some softness has crept in.

You're often the last one to leave the group chat and the first to slip out of the party. At a family dinner you're funny and involved, and then somewhere around dessert you're in the kitchen doing the dishes on your own, because you needed ten minutes where nobody was reading your face. A friend asks how you are and you give them the news, the new job, the move, the plan for the house, and they walk off realising they've no idea how you feel about any of it. A message that wants something emotional from you sits on read for a day while you work out what you actually think. You do have feelings about things, strong ones, the Moon sees to that. You just like to have them in private first and bring them out once they're sorted, which from across the table can look as though you never had them at all.

People tell you things, and the things stay told. That's the part of this decan nobody mentions. The Moon here knows what it is to need a private room, so you treat other people's private rooms with a lot of respect. A friend mentions the IVF, or the job interview they haven't told their boss about, or the fact that their marriage is wobbling, and it goes nowhere. You don't hint at it later, you don't bring it up at the wrong moment, and you don't make them feel watched. You also let people change their minds without holding the old version against them. At work this makes you the one colleagues come to before they hand in their notice. In a family it makes you the sibling who knows everything and says nothing, which is a quiet sort of power, and you mostly use it kindly.

The less obvious shadow is the quiet exit. The man on the card doesn't have a row with the camp, he just goes, and that's your habit when something stops working. You don't tell your flatmate the arrangement is making you miserable. You find another flat, sign the lease, and mention it three weeks before you move. A friendship that's gone sour doesn't get a conversation, it gets slower replies until it fades. Usually you've had good reasons. The trouble is the other person never got a chance to fix anything, and they're left wondering what they did. There's a private story running under it too, the version where leaving quietly is the considerate thing and a fuss would be selfish. Sometimes that's true. Often it's the Seven of Swords telling you a flattering tale about your own motives, and you're clever enough to believe it.

When things go wrong you go practical and very, very private. A redundancy, a break-up, a parent getting ill, and for the first few days you're organised and calm and you tell almost nobody. You make lists. You ring the bank. About a week later you've usually got a whole plan in place, a new job applied for, a room lined up, a solution arrived at alone, and that's the point where the people close to you find out anything happened. Your partner hears about it after your cousin did. That hurts people more than you realise, because they wanted to help and you'd already finished. What actually helps is letting one person in while it's still a mess. Someone you trust, sitting with you over a cup of tea before the plan exists, even though every instinct you have says wait until it's sorted.

You're more sentimental than anyone would guess. The Moon keeps things, so there's probably a shoebox somewhere with ticket stubs and a card from your first serious relationship, and you'd be mortified if a partner found it. You love with a lot of loyalty and very little announcement. What trips you up is testing. Instead of saying you feel neglected, you go a bit quiet and wait to see whether your partner notices, and if they don't, you file it away as evidence. After a year or two there's a whole case built up that they've never heard a word of. The people who suit you are the ones who notice without being told and who don't sulk when you need an evening on your own. And it helps enormously when you say the small hurt out loud on the day it happens.

The Star as your Sun card is about working for something bigger than yourself, and this slice gives it a job that's done mostly out of sight. You're good wherever discretion is the skill. Research, investigative journalism, IT security, audit, negotiation, legal work, HR, being the person who runs the numbers before the big announcement. You see the angle other people miss and you're happy to work it out on your own. The catch is visibility. You don't tell your manager what you're doing until it's done, and in the meantime it can look like you're doing nothing. Then the finished thing arrives and everyone's surprised, and a bit put out that they weren't told. Send a short update halfway through anything that matters, even if it feels premature. It costs you ten minutes and saves you a reputation for going it alone.

At twenty this decan usually shows up as a lot of small, tidy fibs. You were at the library, you're fine, it was nothing. Mostly they're told to avoid fuss, and there's often a quiet drift away from friend groups that nobody quite noticed you leaving. By the mid-thirties most people with a Sun here have worked out the difference between privacy and hiding, usually because hiding cost them something they wanted. They still keep their own counsel, and they've learnt to say the difficult thing before quietly walking off. The fifties often bring out the Pisces edge of these degrees. People tend to soften, become the trusted confidant in the family, the one who knows where everything is buried and has decided none of it needs digging up. The risk then is keeping so much for other people that nobody knows much about you.

Once a week, tell one person one thing while it's still unfinished. A feeling you haven't made sense of, a worry about work you haven't solved, a small hurt from something they said. Say it in the messy version, the way it sits before you've tidied it up, and stop there without offering the plan. Pick someone who's earned it. Notice how they respond, and how much less you have to carry on your own for the rest of the week.
